P.n: Imperial Palace East Gardens (皇居東御苑)
P.w: The free public garden on the old honmaru of Edo Castle — the castle-keep base, guardhouses and a seasonal garden inside the palace walls.
The 1869 Shintō shrine to Japan's war dead — great torii, cherry-tree avenue and the Yūshūkan war museum; politically contested, historically essential.
1,300-year-old shrine of Edo's merchants, home of the Kanda Matsuri — and, a block from Akihabara, an anime pilgrimage stop (Love Live!) with IT-blessing omamori.

P.n: Tokyo Station Marunouchi Building (東京駅丸の内駅舎)
P.w: Tatsuno Kingo's 1914 red-brick station front, restored with its twin domes in 2012 — a nationally Important Cultural Property.

P.n: National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo (MOMAT)
P.w: Japan's first national art museum — the definitive collection of 20th-century Japanese painting (Kishida, Yokoyama Taikan) beside the palace moat.

P.n: Akihabara Electric Town (秋葉原電気街)
P.w: Tokyo's electronics-and-otaku quarter — multi-storey arcades, figure shops, retro-game dens and maid cafés around Chūō-dōri.

P.n: Jimbōchō Book Town (神保町古書店街)
P.w: 100+ second-hand and antiquarian bookshops along Yasukuni-dōri — named Time Out's World's Coolest Neighbourhood 2025; also a curry-rice heartland.
Hilltop shrine of the Sannō Matsuri, reached by an escalator or a tunnel of vermilion torii on its west stair.
The octagonal 1964 Olympic judo hall that became Japan's rock temple (the Beatles, 1966) — still the martial-arts and concert landmark of Kitanomaru Park.
Tokyo's oldest temple (founded 645) — through the Kaminarimon thunder gate and the Nakamise-dōri stall street to the main hall and five-storey pagoda.

P.n: Tokyo National Museum (東京国立博物館)
P.w: Japan's oldest and largest museum — 120,000 objects including 89 National Treasures, from Jōmon pottery to samurai armour and ukiyo-e, in Ueno Park.
Japan's first public park (1873) — museums, the zoo, Shinobazu Pond's lotus beds, Tōshō-gū and Tokyo's most famous cherry-blossom avenue. Free entry.
'Kitchen Town' — some 170 shops between Ueno and Asakusa selling knives, lacquerware, noren and the plastic food samples of every Japanese shop window.
The national sumo hall — three of the six annual grand tournaments (January, May, September) are fought here; the Sumo Museum and the chanko-nabe restaurants of Ryōgoku surround it.

P.n: Sumida Hokusai Museum (すみだ北斎美術館)
P.w: Kazuyo Sejima's faceted aluminium museum (2016) for Hokusai, who spent most of his 88 years in Sumida — his life, his prints and the neighbourhood that shaped them.
Meiji-era stroll garden built by the Iwasaki (Mitsubishi) family — a big pond, stepping stones of prized rock from across Japan, carp, turtles and a lakeside teahouse.
Edo-period shrine in old-town Yanesen with a tunnel of small vermilion torii and a hillside of some 3,000 azaleas each April.

P.n: Shibuya Scramble Crossing (渋谷スクランブル交差点)
P.w: The world's busiest pedestrian crossing — up to 3,000 people per green light outside Shibuya Station and the Hachikō statue; watch it from Shibuya Sky or the station's upper floors.
Big, informal park beside Meiji Jingū — weekend buskers, rockabilly dancers, ginkgo avenues in autumn and festivals on the event plaza.

P.n: Shinjuku Gyoen National Garden (新宿御苑)
P.w: Former imperial garden blending French formal, English landscape and Japanese styles — 1,000 cherry trees, a tropical greenhouse and a teahouse, minutes from Shinjuku Station.

P.n: Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building (東京都庁)
P.w: Kenzo Tange's twin-towered city hall with free 202 m observation decks — Mt Fuji on clear winter mornings and an evening projection-mapping show on the facade.

P.n: Shinjuku Golden Gai (新宿ゴールデン街)
P.w: Six narrow lanes of 200-odd postwar shoebox bars, each seating a handful — the most atmospheric drinking quarter in Tokyo.
Shrine to Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken in a 70-hectare planted forest between Harajuku and Yoyogi — giant cypress torii, sake-barrel wall, and Japan's busiest New Year hatsumōde.

P.n: Tokyo Skytree (東京スカイツリー)
P.w: At 634 m the world's tallest tower — observation decks at 350 m and 450 m, with Tokyo Solamachi mall and an aquarium at its foot.
Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu's 1702 stroll garden recreating 88 scenes from waka poetry — a weeping cherry in spring and lantern-lit maples in autumn.
Tokyo's oldest daimyō garden (1629, Mito Tokugawa) — the Engetsu-kyō full-moon bridge, plum grove and miniature Chinese and Japanese landscapes beside Tokyo Dome.
Tokyo's grand kabuki theatre behind a Momoyama-style facade — buy a single-act makumi ticket on the day to sample a play from the top gallery.
The 1911 granite bridge at 'kilometre zero' of Japan's roads — the start of the Edo-period Tōkaidō, bronze kirin on its lamps, the expressway overhead soon to be buried.
Shōgun's former duck-hunting garden on Tokyo Bay with a tidal seawater pond and the Nakajima teahouse for matcha, ringed by Shiodome towers.
The Tokugawa shōguns' family temple — the 1622 Sangedatsumon gate, rows of jizō statues in knitted caps, and Tokyo Tower rising directly behind the main hall.

P.n: Roppongi Hills Mori Tower — Tokyo City View & Mori Art Museum
P.w: The 54-storey heart of Roppongi Hills: the Mori Art Museum's contemporary shows and the Tokyo City View deck on the 52nd floor.
P.k: Mori Art Museum, Tokyo City View

P.w: Barefoot immersive digital-art museum in Toyosu — wade knee-deep through projected koi, a floating-flower dome and a mirrored infinity crystal universe.
Tokyo's wholesale fish market since 2018 — watch the dawn tuna auction from the observation gallery, then sushi breakfast in the market restaurants.
Fukagawa's great Hachiman shrine — birthplace of Edo kanjin sumo (the yokozuna monument stands here) and host of the water-splashing Fukagawa Hachiman festival.
Japan's major public contemporary-art museum, in Kiba Park near Kiyosumi-Shirakawa's coffee roasters.

P.n: Nakano Broadway (中野ブロードウェイ)
P.w: 1966 shopping-and-apartment complex turned otaku mecca — four floors of Mandarake, vintage toys, manga, idol goods and watch dealers at the end of Nakano Sun Mall.
Tokyo's bohemian village of vintage-clothing shops, tiny theatres, live houses and coffee stands around Shimo-kitazawa Station and the Ichibangai shopping street.
The 333 m orange-and-white 1958 lattice tower — Main Deck at 150 m and Top Deck at 250 m, and still the city's favourite night-skyline icon.
Small Takanawa temple holding the graves of the 47 rōnin of Akō — incense is still lit at each grave, and a festival marks their vendetta every 14 December.

P.n: Ghibli Museum, Mitaka (三鷹の森ジブリ美術館)
P.w: Hayao Miyazaki's own whimsical museum on the edge of Inokashira Park — animation workshops, a Catbus room, a rooftop Laputa robot and short films shown only here. Advance tickets only.
Kichijōji's beloved park — swan boats on a cherry-lined pond, the Benzaiten shrine and weekend craft stalls, a short walk from the Ghibli Museum.
599 m sacred mountain an hour from Shinjuku — cable car or trails up to Yakuō-in temple and a summit view of Mt Fuji on clear days.
Tokyo's second-oldest temple (733) in a spring-fed forest, ringed by soba shops making Jindai-ji soba from the local water.

P.n: Great Buddha of Kamakura — Kōtoku-in (鎌倉大仏)
P.w: The 13.35 m bronze Amida Buddha (1252) sitting in the open air since a 15th-century tsunami washed its hall away — you can step inside the hollow statue.
Kamakura's central shrine, founded by Minamoto no Yoritomo — a grand approach from the sea up Dankazura, lotus ponds and a hilltop main hall.
Tokugawa Ieyasu's lavishly carved mausoleum shrine in cedar forest — the Yōmeimon gate, the three wise monkeys and the sleeping cat; part of the UNESCO Shrines and Temples of Nikkō.
Daikyō-ji, the shitamachi temple of the 'Tora-san' films — its halls wrapped in astonishing wood-carved panels, reached down the Taishakuten-sandō street of kusa-dango and senbei shops.

P.n: Kasai Rinkai Park (葛西臨海公園)
P.w: Bayside park with a giant Ferris wheel, a bird sanctuary, a beach and the Tokyo Sea Life Park aquarium's tuna doughnut tank.

P.n: Holy Resurrection Cathedral — Nikolai-dō (ニコライ堂)
P.w: Green-domed 1891 Byzantine-style Orthodox cathedral founded by St Nicholas of Japan, rising unexpectedly over Ochanomizu.

P.n: Tokyo International Forum (東京国際フォーラム)
P.w: Rafael Viñoly's 1996 glass-hull atrium between Yūrakuchō and Tokyo Station — free to walk through, with a weekend antique market on the plaza.

P.n: Shibuya Sky — Shibuya Scramble Square (渋谷スカイ)
P.ad: Shibuya Scramble Square, Shibuya 2-chōme, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo
P.w: Open-air rooftop deck 230 m above the Scramble Crossing on top of the 2019 Shibuya Scramble Square tower — sunset over Mt Fuji is the prize.
Bronze of the Akita who waited at Shibuya Station for his dead master for nearly ten years — Tokyo's most famous meeting point.

P.n: Yebisu Garden Place (恵比寿ガーデンプレイス)
P.w: Plaza on the site of the old Yebisu brewery — the beer's birthplace brewery restarted here, plus the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum and a Baccarat chandelier each winter.
Tadao Ando's spiral-ramp mall on the zelkova-lined Omotesandō boulevard — the avenue of architect-designed flagships between Harajuku and Aoyama.
Kengo Kuma's bamboo-lined museum of pre-modern Asian art (Kōrin's Irises screen each spring) with a deep, hilly stroll garden and teahouses behind.

P.n: The National Art Center, Tokyo (国立新美術館)
P.w: Kisho Kurokawa's undulating glass-facade exhibition hall in Roppongi — Japan's largest exhibition space, no permanent collection, a cone-top café.

P.n: Kyū-Shiba-rikyū Gardens (旧芝離宮恩賜庭園)
P.w: One of Tokyo's oldest daimyō stroll gardens (1678), a pond landscape tucked beside Hamamatsuchō Station.

P.n: Rainbow Bridge (レインボーブリッジ)
P.w: Suspension bridge to Odaiba with a free pedestrian promenade on each side — the classic view back to the Tokyo skyline and Tokyo Tower, lit at night.

P.n: National Museum of Western Art (国立西洋美術館)
P.w: Le Corbusier's only building in East Asia — part of the UNESCO Le Corbusier serial site — housing the Matsukata collection of Rodin, Monet and Old Masters; Rodin's Gates of Hell stand in the forecourt.
Josiah Conder's 1896 Jacobean-style mansion for the Mitsubishi Iwasaki family, with a Japanese wing and a Swiss-chalet billiard house — Meiji Westernisation in one garden.
Leafy old cemetery of shōguns' retainers and Meiji notables — cherry-tree avenues, the last shōgun Tokugawa Yoshinobu's tomb and the neighbourhood's resident cats.
The 1649 Gongen-style shrine beside Sensō-ji honouring the temple's three founders, home of the riotous Sanja Matsuri each May.
Josiah Conder's stone Western villa above a terraced rose garden that steps down to a Japanese pond garden by Ogawa Jihei — spectacular at the May and October rose festivals.

P.n: Sunshine City, Ikebukuro (サンシャインシティ)
P.w: Ikebukuro's mega-complex — the rooftop Sunshine Aquarium with its 'sky penguins', Namjatown, the Pokémon Center Mega Tokyo and the Sunshine 60 observatory — next to Otome Road.

P.n: Jiyū Gakuen Myōnichikan (自由学園明日館)
P.w: Frank Lloyd Wright's 1921 Prairie-style school building with Arata Endo — an Important Cultural Property where you can take tea in the double-height hall.

P.n: Meguro Parasitological Museum (目黒寄生虫館)
P.w: Free, gloriously odd private museum of some 300 parasite specimens — the star is an 8.8 m tapeworm.

P.n: Tokyo Metropolitan Teien Art Museum (東京都庭園美術館)
P.w: Prince Asaka's 1933 Art Deco residence — Lalique glass doors, Henri Rapin interiors — used as an exhibition museum inside a Japanese and Western garden.
The 'cat temple' said to be the birthplace of the maneki-neko — thousands of white beckoning cats lined up beside the hall, under a 22.5 m three-tiered pagoda.
Hilltop head temple of Nichiren Buddhism on the site where Nichiren died in 1282 — with the oldest five-storey pagoda in the Kantō region.

P.n: CupNoodles Museum Yokohama (カップヌードルミュージアム 横浜)
P.w: Momofuku Ando's instant-noodle museum in Minato Mirai — design your own Cup Noodle to take home, or hand-make chicken ramen from scratch.

P.n: Yokohama Landmark Tower — Sky Garden (横浜ランドマークタワー)
P.w: Minato Mirai's 296 m tower with the Sky Garden observatory on the 69th floor over Yokohama Bay, Mt Fuji on clear days.
Cedar-shaded shrine on Lake Ashi whose red 'torii of peace' stands in the water — the classic Hakone photograph.

P.n: Hakone Open-Air Museum (彫刻の森美術館)
P.ad: Hakone, Ashigarashimo District, Kanagawa (by Chōkoku-no-Mori Station)
P.w: Japan's first open-air art museum — Moore and Rodin on mountain lawns, a stained-glass Symphonic Sculpture tower, a Picasso pavilion and a hot-spring foot bath.
Hillside temple of the 9 m eleven-headed Kannon, with sea views over Yuigahama, a cave of carved deities and a famous hydrangea path in June.
Second of Kamakura's Five Great Zen Temples (1282), a forested complex by Kita-Kamakura Station holding the National Treasure Shariden relic hall.
Japan's oldest Zen training monastery (1253) and first of Kamakura's Five Mountains — great gate, juniper garden and a hike up to Hansōbō's tengu statues.
Small Zen temple behind a grove of 2,000 Mōsō bamboo, with matcha served in a tea pavilion inside the grove.
Tidal island off Shōnan's surf beaches — Enoshima Shrine, the Sea Candle lighthouse, the Iwaya caves and shirasu-don stalls, with Mt Fuji across Sagami Bay.

P.ad: Chūgūshi, Nikkō, Tochigi (outflow of Lake Chūzenji)
P.w: 97 m waterfall draining Lake Chūzenji — an elevator drops to a platform at the base of the plunge; ranked among Japan's three finest falls.
Nikkō's chief Tendai temple, founded by Shōdō Shōnin — three giant gilded Buddhas in the Sanbutsu-dō and the Taiyūin mausoleum of the third shōgun; part of the UNESCO Nikkō site.
High lake at the foot of sacred Mt Nantai, ringed by autumn colour, old embassy villas and Chūzen-ji temple — reached by the hairpin Irohazaka road.

P.n: Chūreitō Pagoda — Arakurayama Sengen Park (忠霊塔)
P.w: The five-storey pagoda framed against Mt Fuji — 398 steps up from Shimoyoshida; cherry blossom in April and autumn maples make it Japan's most-photographed view.
The most accessible of the Fuji Five Lakes — Fuji reflected on the north shore, the Kachi Kachi ropeway and lakeside onsen ryokan.
Eight crystal spring ponds fed by Fuji snowmelt in a thatched-roof village between Kawaguchiko and Yamanakako.
Kawagoe's great Tendai temple — rooms moved from Edo Castle (including Iemitsu's birth chamber) and the 540 Gohyaku Rakan stone disciples, each face different.

P.n: Toki no Kane — Kawagoe Time Bell (時の鐘)
P.w: Wooden bell tower rising over the kurazukuri clay-walled merchant houses of 'Little Edo' — still rung four times a day.

P.n: Yayoi Kusama Museum (草間彌生美術館)
P.w: Five-storey white museum devoted to Kusama — polka dots, pumpkins and an infinity-mirror room; timed tickets sell out in advance.
Shinjuku's guardian shrine beside Golden Gai — the Tori-no-Ichi rake fairs in November and a Sunday antique market under the trees.

P.n: Tokyu Kabukichō Tower (東急歌舞伎町タワー)
P.w: 2023 entertainment tower in the heart of Kabukichō — theatre, a neon 'Shinjuku Kabuki Hall' food hall of yokochō stalls and rooftop views; the Godzilla head looms next door.
Sloping old geisha quarter with cobbled back alleys of ryōtei, a French-expat bistro scene and Zenkoku-ji's Bishamonten at its crest.
Startling 1934 Indian-style Buddhist temple by Itō Chūta, with a pipe organ inside and a breakfast café — at the gate of the Tsukiji outer market.
Nihonbashi shrine for safe childbirth — expectant parents queue on the 'Day of the Dog'; Ningyōchō's ningyō-yaki stalls are a block away.
The 1932 neo-Renaissance Seiko clock tower on the Ginza 4-chōme crossing — Ginza's emblem since the Shōwa era, with luxury floors below.
Tokyo's largest waterside park — poplar avenues along the Koaidame reservoir, a metasequoia forest and 200,000 irises in June.

P.n: Edo-Tokyo Open Air Architectural Museum (江戸東京たてもの園)
P.w: Thirty rescued historic buildings in Koganei Park — Edo farmhouses, a Shōwa sentō and shop row that inspired Spirited Away, and Maekawa Kunio's modernist home.

P.n: Shōwa Kinen Park (国営昭和記念公園)
P.w: Vast national memorial park in Tachikawa — seasonal flower fields (tulips, cosmos), a golden ginkgo avenue, a Japanese garden and bike paths.
The largest limestone cave in the Kantō, deep in the Okutama mountains — a steady 11 °C walk past stalactites and a lit 'Hall of the Gods'.

Punk-and-vintage Chūō Line neighbourhood of used-clothing shops, tiny live houses, izakaya under the tracks and the huge Awa-odori dance festival every August — named one of the world's coolest neighbourhoods by Time Out in 2026.

P.n: Nakameguro & the Meguro River (中目黒・目黒川)
P.w: Canal-side neighbourhood of boutiques, coffee bars and izakaya under the tracks; in early April 800 cherry trees arch over the Meguro River and the lanterns come out.
Genteel residential shopping town famed for patisseries and the 'Sweets Forest' dessert hall, plus La Vita's mini-Venice canal.

P.n: Meguro Sky Garden (目黒天空庭園)
P.w: A looping rooftop park built on top of the Ōhashi expressway junction — 7,000 m² of gardens 35 m up, with sunset views toward Fuji.
Shōgun Tsunayoshi's 1681 temple for his mother — one of the few great Edo-period halls to survive earthquake and war intact, quiet and rarely visited.

P.n: Tokyo Dome City (東京ドームシティ)
P.w: Home of the Yomiuri Giants (55,000 seats) plus a roller coaster that threads through a building, the LaQua spa and the Japanese Baseball Hall of Fame.
Black-lacquered Confucian temple founded by the shōguns' Confucian scholars — the Edo academy where samurai officials were trained; giant bronze Confucius in the grounds.
Silk merchant Hara Sankei's stroll garden of historic buildings moved from Kyoto, Kamakura and Gifu — a three-storey pagoda over the pond and a gasshō farmhouse.
Japan's largest Chinatown — ten ornate gates, the Kantei-byō and Ma Zu temples and 500-odd shops steaming nikuman and xiaolongbao.
Japan's first Western-style park (1903), across the moat from the Imperial Palace — rose beds, an open-air concert hall and the century-old Matsumoto-rō restaurant.
The stepped-pyramid granite parliament (1936) — free guided tours of the House of Councillors chamber run on weekdays.
Wooded former Edo Castle enclosure north of the palace — the Budōkan, the Science Museum and MOMAT among cherry trees by the Chidorigafuchi moat.
Postwar black-market street under the Yamanote tracks between Ueno and Okachimachi — fishmongers shouting year-end deals, dried goods, spices, sneakers and standing izakaya.
'Memory Lane' — a smoky postwar alley of yakitori and motsu-yaki counters squeezed against the tracks at Shinjuku's west exit.
Harajuku's 400 m teen-fashion street opposite the station — crêpes, kawaii shops, rainbow candy floss and weekend crowds shoulder to shoulder.

P.n: Katsushika Shibamata Tora-san Museum (葛飾柴又寅さん記念館)
P.w: Museum of the 48-film 'Otoko wa Tsurai yo' saga — the Kurumaya dango shop set and props from the films shot in Shibamata from 1969 to 1995.

P.n: KochiKame Museum, Kameari (こち亀記念館)
P.w: Compact museum for Osamu Akimoto's 200-volume manga 'KochiKame: Tokyo Beat Cops', recreating the Kameari Park police box — start of a trail of bronze statues of Ryōtsu and friends around Kameari Station.
Sōji-ji, the great Shingon temple of Adachi (founded 826) — peony gardens, kusa-dango stalls at the gate and a February daruma-burning rite.

P.n: Yoyogi National Gymnasium (国立代々木競技場)
P.w: Kenzo Tange's soaring suspension-roof arenas for the 1964 Olympics — a landmark of Japanese modernism beside Yoyogi Park.

P.n: Daikanyama T-Site — Tsutaya Books (代官山 蔦屋書店)
P.w: Klein Dytham's woven-T bookshop pavilions in leafy Daikanyama — magazines, the Anjin lounge and cafés; a design-lover's half-day.
Shibuya's 2020 linear rooftop park over a mall — skate park, lawn, and the Shibuya Yokochō food-stall alley underneath.

P.n: Fukagawa Edo Museum (深川江戸資料館)
P.w: A full-scale walk-through Fukagawa street of 1840 — tenements, a rice shop, a boathouse and a cat on the roof, with the light shifting from dawn to dusk.
A townsman's flower garden laid out in 1804 for Edo poets — plum blossom in February and a tunnel of bush clover (hagi) in September.

P.n: Tokyo Big Sight (東京ビッグサイト)
P.w: The inverted-pyramid convention centre on the bay — home of Comiket, AnimeJapan and the Design Festa, the city's biggest pop-culture crowds.

P.n: Unicorn Gundam Statue, DiverCity Tokyo Plaza — CLOSED
P.ad: DiverCity Tokyo Plaza, Aomi, Kōtō-ku, Tokyo
P.w: The life-size 19.7 m transforming Unicorn Gundam outside DiverCity in Odaiba (2017–2026) — Time Out reported it would be retired in August 2026; the Gundam Base shop remains inside.

P.n: Godzilla Head, Hotel Gracery Shinjuku (ゴジラヘッド)
P.w: A life-size Godzilla head glowering over Kabukichō from the Shinjuku Tōhō Building's 8th-floor terrace — it roars and glows on the hour.

P.n: Shin-Ōkubo Koreatown (新大久保コリアンタウン)
P.w: Tokyo's K-culture strip around Shin-Ōkubo Station — cheese hotteok, K-beauty and idol shops, plus the halal grocers of 'Islam Yokochō'.

P.n: Meiji Jingū Gaien & Ichō Namiki Ginkgo Avenue (明治神宮外苑 いちょう並木)
P.ad: Meiji Jingū Gaien, 1-1 Kasumigaokamachi, Shinjuku-ku, Tokyo (ginkgo avenue runs in from Aoyama-dōri)
P.w: The Outer Garden's 300 m double row of 146 ginkgo trees that turns pure gold in late November — Tokyo's most famous autumn avenue, leading to the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery.
Steaming volcanic valley of sulphur vents on the Hakone Ropeway — eat a black kuro-tamago egg boiled in the hot springs, said to add seven years to your life.
Hakone's caldera lake crossed by mock pirate ships between Tōgendai and Moto-Hakone, with Mt Fuji over the far shore on clear days.

P.n: Akihabara Radio Kaikan (秋葉原ラジオ会館)
P.ad: Off the Electric Town exit of JR Akihabara Station, Sotokanda, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo
P.w: Akihabara's ten floors of otaku culture by the station — figures, trading cards, model kits, gacha machines and K-Books.
Hands-on Japan Science Foundation museum in Kitanomaru Park — five floors of experiments, bikes, robots and electricity shows for kids.

P.n: Setagaya Boro-ichi & Daikan Yashiki (世田谷ボロ市・代官屋敷)
P.w: A 440-year-old flea market filling Boro-ichi-dōri every 15–16 December and 15–16 January, around the thatched Edo-period magistrate's residence (Daikan Yashiki).
Former estate of music critic Ōtaguro Motoo in Ogikubo — a ginkgo-lined approach, pond garden and a free autumn-leaf light-up.
Hōjō clan stronghold that fell to Hideyoshi in 1590 — the 1960 rebuilt keep is the nearest castle tower to Tokyo, on the way to Hakone.

P.n: Fujiya Hotel, Miyanoshita (富士屋ホテル)
P.w: Japan's first Western-style resort hotel (1878) — Chaplin, Helen Keller and royalty stayed; the temple-roofed buildings and old dining hall are a Hakone landmark.

P.n: Asakura Museum of Sculpture (朝倉彫塑館)
P.w: Sculptor Fumio Asakura's 1935 studio-home in Yanaka — a sukiya house around a stone water garden, with bronze cats and a rooftop garden over the old town.
Japan's oldest zoo (1882) inside Ueno Park — famous for its giant pandas, plus a five-storey pagoda left from Kan'ei-ji in the grounds.
Gold-leafed 1651 shrine to Tokugawa Ieyasu in Ueno Park, approached past 200 stone and bronze lanterns; peony garden in winter and spring.
Japan's oldest amusement park (1853), a pocket-sized retro funfair behind Sensō-ji with a 1953 roller coaster that skims the neighbours' roofs.
Shrine atop Atago-yama, the highest natural point in central Tokyo, reached by the 86 brutally steep 'Stairs of Success' that a samurai once rode up on horseback.

P.n: Azabudai Hills & teamLab Borderless (麻布台ヒルズ)
P.w: Mori Building's 2023 hillside district crowned by Japan's tallest skyscraper, with Heatherwick-designed garden pavilions and the relocated teamLab Borderless digital-art museum in its basement.

P.ad: Toranomon Hills Mori Tower, 1-23-4 Toranomon, Minato-ku, Tokyo
P.w: Four-tower Mori district over its own Hibiya Line station — the T-Market food hall, rooftop TOKYO NODE gallery and the Andaz hotel bar.

P.n: Shinjuku Central Park (新宿中央公園)
P.w: Green lung among the Nishi-Shinjuku skyscrapers — the Kumano Jūnisha shrine, a waterfall plaza and Shukunohara café lawns beside the Metropolitan Government Building.

P.n: Tokyo Opera City (東京オペラシティ)
P.w: Hatsudai arts complex — the pyramid-roofed Takemitsu concert hall, the Opera City Art Gallery and the NTT InterCommunication Center media-art space.
Ginza's biggest department complex (2017) on the old Matsuzakaya site — a vast free rooftop garden, the Tsutaya art-book hall and a deep basement food floor.

P.ad: Near the summit of Mt. Takao, Takaomachi, Hachiōji, Tokyo
P.w: Mountain temple of the Shugendō ascetics just below Takao's summit — long-nosed tengu statues, an octopus-root cedar and the March fire-walking festival.
Mountain-top Hōjō castle stormed in 1590 — restored stone walls, a rebuilt bridge and the Gotenzawa palace site on a wooded hiking trail; one of Japan's 100 Fine Castles.

P.n: Tama Zoological Park (多摩動物公園)
P.w: Hillside zoo where animals roam large open enclosures — the lion bus drives through the lion zone, plus a famous insectarium of butterflies.

P.ad: Sumida River banks, Taitō-ku / Sumida-ku, Tokyo (by Tokyo Mizumachi)
P.w: Riverside promenade below Asakusa — a kilometre of cherry trees with Skytree across the water, the July Sumida River fireworks and the Tokyo Mizumachi river walk bridge.
Small Edo-period daimyō stroll garden once fed by the tides of the Sumida, beside the Kokugikan — free and rarely crowded.

P.ad: Tokyo Skytree Town Solamachi 5–6F, 1-1-2 Oshiage, Sumida-ku, Tokyo 131-0045
P.w: Indoor aquarium at the foot of Skytree — Magellanic penguins in an open pool, a jellyfish chamber and Edo-style goldfish.

P.n: Warner Bros. Studio Tour Tokyo — The Making of Harry Potter
P.w: Asia's only Harry Potter studio tour (2023) on the old Toshimaen site — the Great Hall, Diagon Alley, the Hogwarts Express and the Ministry of Magic sets; timed tickets.
Shōgun Yoshimune's 18th-century cherry hill for commoners — some 650 trees, three museums (incl. the Shibusawa Memorial Museum), an old tram car and a free mini-monorail up the slope.
One of Tokyo's largest green spaces around the Sanpōji and Shakujii ponds — boating, spring-fed wetlands and picnics under the cherries.

P.n: Ōji Inari Shrine (王子稲荷神社)
P.w: Head Inari shrine of the Kantō — legend says foxes gather here in human form on New Year's Eve, now re-enacted in the lantern-lit Ōji Fox Parade.
Shrine to the scholar-god Sugawara no Michizane with drum bridges over a pond — famous for the April–May wisteria trellises framing Skytree.
Taishō-era merchant house blending Japanese and Western rooms around a celebrated shoin garden — matcha on the tatami beside the Taishakuten.

P.n: Horikiri Shōbuen Iris Garden (堀切菖蒲園)
P.w: Edo-era iris garden painted by Hiroshige — some 6,000 plants of 200 varieties bloom in June for the Katsushika Iris Festival. Free.

P.n: Ukiyo-e Ōta Memorial Museum of Art (太田記念美術館)
P.w: Seizō Ōta's 15,000-print ukiyo-e collection — Hokusai, Hiroshige, Utamaro — shown in rotating monthly exhibitions in a hushed house a step off Omotesandō; shoes off at the door.

P.n: Watari-um Museum of Contemporary Art (ワタリウム美術館)
P.w: Mario Botta's striped wedge of a gallery (1990) on Gaien-nishi-dōri, with four contemporary shows a year and the excellent On Sundays art bookshop.

P.n: Setagaya Art Museum (世田谷美術館)
P.w: Museum in leafy Kinuta Park with 18,000 works — strong on outsider and naïve art and Setagaya's own artists.

P.n: Artizon Museum (アーティゾン美術館)
P.w: The former Bridgestone Museum, rebuilt in 2020 near Tokyo Station — Impressionists, Japanese Western-style painting and contemporary shows.
Neighbourhood aquarium in Shinagawa Kumin Park — a walk-through tunnel tank, seal and dolphin shows, cheaper and calmer than the big-name aquariums.

P.n: Tokyo Port Wild Bird Park (東京港野鳥公園)
P.ad: Tōkai, Ōta-ku, Tokyo (Tokyo Bay shore, on the Tokyo Monorail)
P.w: Reclaimed-land wetland reserve on Tokyo Bay with hides over tidal flats — herons, plovers and migrating shorebirds between the container docks and Haneda.
Broad western-Setagaya park of lawns and cherry trees around the Setagaya Art Museum — Tokyo families' favourite hanami picnic ground.
Kaminoge museum of the Tōkyū founder's collection — Heian scrolls of the Tale of Genji (shown each spring) and a steep wooded garden of stone lanterns.

P.n: Hasegawa Machiko Art Museum (長谷川町子美術館)
P.w: Museum of the creator of 'Sazae-san' in Sakura-shinmachi, whose station street is lined with statues of the Isono family.

P.n: Seikadō Bunko Art Museum (静嘉堂文庫美術館)
P.w: The Iwasaki family's treasure collection — including a National Treasure yōhen tenmoku tea bowl — now shown in the 1934 Meiji Seimei-kan in Marunouchi.
The Hosokawa daimyō family's treasure house in a 1930s office building above Higo-Hosokawa Garden — armour, tea wares and Zen paintings.

P.n: Tōyō Bunko Museum (東洋文庫ミュージアム)
P.w: Japan's great Oriental library — the floor-to-ceiling 'Morrison Library' wall of 24,000 books and rare maps, next to Rikugien.
Free daimyō pond garden on the Kanda River slope where the Hosokawa lords had their Edo villa — with the Shōseikaku tea pavilion.
Hotel garden on Yamagata Aritomo's old estate — a three-storey pagoda, camellias, summer fireflies and a dry-ice 'sea of clouds' rolling over the lawns.

P.n: State Guest House, Akasaka Palace (迎賓館赤坂離宮)
P.w: Japan's only neo-Baroque palace (1909), the state guesthouse for visiting heads of state and a National Treasure — open to the public on most days for its gilded halls and fountain garden.

P.n: Tokyo Midtown (東京ミッドタウン)
P.w: Roppongi's 2007 complex on the old Defence Agency site — Hinokichō Park, the galleria and two design museums in its grounds.

P.n: Suntory Museum of Art (サントリー美術館)
P.ad: Tokyo Midtown Galleria 3F, 9-7-4 Akasaka, Minato-ku, Tokyo 107-8643
P.w: Kengo Kuma-designed museum of Japanese decorative art — lacquer, glass, ceramics and screens — under the theme 'Art in Life'.

P.ad: Tokyo Midtown Garden, 9-7-6 Akasaka, Minato-ku, Tokyo 107-0052
P.w: Tadao Ando's folded-steel-roof design gallery conceived with Issey Miyake, half-buried in Midtown's garden.

P.ad: Kiba, Kōtō-ku, Tokyo (park containing the Museum of Contemporary Art Tokyo)
P.w: Former timber-yard park in Kōtō with a suspension footbridge, Skytree views and the Museum of Contemporary Art at its edge; October brings the Kiba log-rolling (kakunori) show.

P.n: Yokohama Red Brick Warehouse (横浜赤レンガ倉庫)
P.ad: Shinkō, Naka-ku, Yokohama, Kanagawa (Port of Yokohama)
P.w: Two 1910s customs warehouses on the Yokohama waterfront turned into shops, a hall and the venue for Oktoberfest and the winter Christmas market.

P.n: Zeniarai Benten, Kamakura (銭洗弁財天宇賀福神社)
P.ad: Sasuke, Kamakura, Kanagawa (west of Kamakura Station)
P.w: Cave shrine reached through a rock tunnel and torii, where visitors wash their coins in spring water to make them multiply.

P.n: Futarasan Shrine, Nikkō (日光二荒山神社)
P.w: Shrine to Nikkō's three sacred mountains, older than Tōshō-gū — it owns the vermilion Shinkyō bridge at the gateway to the UNESCO precinct.

P.n: Kōkyo Gaien & Nijūbashi (皇居外苑・二重橋)
P.ad: Kōkyo Gaien, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo (in front of the Imperial Palace)
P.w: The Imperial Palace's outer garden — a gravel plaza of 2,000 sculpted black pines leading to the classic view of the Nijūbashi bridges and Fushimi turret over the moat.

P.n: Mitsubishi Ichigōkan Museum (三菱一号館美術館)
P.w: A faithful 2009 rebuild of Josiah Conder's 1894 red-brick Mitsubishi office, now a museum of 19th-century European art beside the Brick Square garden.

P.n: Marunouchi Building (丸の内ビルディング)
P.w: The 'Maru-biru' facing Tokyo Station — free 5th-floor terrace views over the restored station dome and restaurant floors up to the 36th.
Sensō-ji's 'Thunder Gate' with its 700 kg red paper lantern and the wind and thunder gods — the start of Nakamise-dōri and Tokyo's most photographed gateway.

P.n: Tokyo Metropolitan Art Museum (東京都美術館)
P.w: Kunio Maekawa's brick museum in Ueno Park hosting Tokyo's blockbuster special exhibitions and the big public art-society shows.

P.n: National Museum of Nature and Science (国立科学博物館)
P.w: Japan's national science museum in Ueno Park — dinosaur halls, Hachikō's preserved body, a Zero fighter and a rooftop herb garden.
The ancient sōja shrine of Musashi Province (founded 111 by tradition) behind a zelkova avenue — home of the night-time Kurayami Matsuri every May.
Ogōchi Dam reservoir deep in the Okutama mountains — floating 'drum bridges', cherry and autumn colour, and the Water and Green Fureai Museum.

P.n: Bishamonten Zenkoku-ji (毘沙門天 善國寺)
P.w: The red-gated temple at the heart of Kagurazaka, guardian of the old geisha quarter and focus of its monthly ennichi fairs.
The Tokyo branch of Ise, where the first Shintō wedding was held in 1901 — now the city's favourite shrine for praying for love, with matchmaking omikuji.
Tokyo branch of Narita-san Shinshō-ji in Monzen-Nakachō — daily goma fire rituals with taiko drums, and a hall wrapped in Sanskrit lettering.

P.n: Odaiba Marine Park (お台場海浜公園)
P.w: Artificial beach on Tokyo Bay facing Rainbow Bridge and the skyline — a mini Statue of Liberty, sunset strolls and the night view back over the water.

P.n: Fuji TV Building — Hachitama observation sphere (フジテレビ本社ビル)
P.w: Kenzo Tange's lattice HQ in Odaiba with the 1.2-ton titanium 'Hachitama' sphere — a 270° view over Tokyo Bay and Rainbow Bridge.

P.n: Institute for Nature Study (国立科学博物館附属自然教育園)
P.w: A fenced-off fragment of primeval Musashino forest and marsh near Meguro Station — admission is capped so the trails stay quiet.

P.n: Nakano Sun Mall (中野サンモール)
P.w: 224 m covered shopping arcade running from Nakano Station's north exit straight into Nakano Broadway.
Nishi-Shinjuku museum that owns one of Van Gogh's 'Sunflowers' (bought in 1987) — shown permanently alongside Seiji Tōgō's paintings.

P.n: National Shōwa Memorial Museum — Shōwa-kan (昭和館)
P.w: Museum of everyday life in wartime and postwar Japan (1935–1955) — ration books, school bags, black-market goods and the home front, by Kudanshita Station.

P.n: Taro Okamoto Memorial Museum (岡本太郎記念館)
P.w: The Expo '70 Tower of the Sun artist's own studio-house in Aoyama — his garden of exuberant sculptures and the atelier left as he worked in it.

P.n: Japan Folk Crafts Museum — Mingeikan (日本民藝館)
P.w: Yanagi Sōetsu's 1936 house-museum of the mingei movement — anonymous everyday crafts, Korean ceramics and Okinawan textiles in a stone-roofed building.

P.n: Fujiko F. Fujio Museum — Doraemon Museum (藤子・F・不二雄ミュージアム)
P.w: Museum of Doraemon's creator in Kawasaki — original manga drawings, a rooftop 'Dokodemo Door' and the Doraemon café; timed advance tickets.

P.n: Nihon Minka-en Open Air Museum (日本民家園)
P.w: Two dozen traditional farmhouses rescued from across eastern Japan — including thatched gasshō houses from Shirakawa-gō — set on a wooded hillside in Ikuta Ryokuchi.

P.n: Kawagoe Hikawa Shrine (川越氷川神社)
P.ad: Kawagoe, Saitama (north of the Kurazukuri street)
P.w: 1,500-year-old shrine of marriage in Kawagoe — a giant wooden torii, fish-shaped fortune 'fishing', and a summer tunnel of thousands of wind chimes.

P.n: Nintendo TOKYO & Pokémon Center Shibuya (Shibuya PARCO 6F)
P.w: 'Cyberspace Shibuya' on PARCO's 6th floor — Nintendo's only official Tokyo store beside the Pokémon Center with its life-size Mewtwo; expect queues.
2012 tower directly over Shibuya Station's east side — ShinQs food hall in the basement and free 11th-floor views back over the crossing.
Ikebukuro's 'Maiden Road' behind Sunshine City — the heart of women's otaku culture, with Animate, K-Books, butler cafés and character-goods stores.
'Harajuku for grannies' — a retro shopping street of red underwear, salt daifuku and senbei around Kōgan-ji, whose Togenuki Jizō is washed by visitors hoping to heal what ails them.
Taishō-era villa garden on the Kokubunji escarpment — a spring-fed pond below a bamboo grove and a hillside of wildflowers; a national Place of Scenic Beauty.

P.n: Jindai Botanical Gardens (神代植物公園)
P.w: Tokyo's big botanical garden beside Jindai-ji — a formal rose garden at its peak in May and October, a tropical greenhouse and plum, azalea and camellia groves.

P.ad: Sekinochō / Sakurachō, Koganei, Tokyo (spans into Kodaira & Nishitōkyō)
P.w: One of Tokyo's largest parks — 1,700 cherry trees around wide lawns and home of the Edo-Tokyo Open Air Architectural Museum.

P.n: Toyosu Senkyaku Banrai (豊洲 千客万来)
P.ad: Toyosu 6-chōme, Kōtō-ku, Tokyo (outer area of Toyosu Market)
P.w: Edo-townscape food street and 24-hour hot-spring spa (2024) next to Toyosu Market — market-fresh sushi and kaisen-don below, a rooftop foot bath facing the bay.

P.n: Yumenoshima Tropical Greenhouse Dome (夢の島熱帯植物館)
P.w: Three glass domes of tropical plants heated by the neighbouring waste-incineration plant, on the reclaimed 'Dream Island'.

P.n: Tokyo Sea Life Park (葛西臨海水族園)
P.w: Glass-domed aquarium in Kasai Rinkai Park famous for its doughnut tank of circling bluefin tuna, plus penguins and a Tokyo Bay gallery.

P.n: Hotel Gajoen Tokyo — Hyakudan Kaidan (ホテル雅叙園東京 百段階段)
P.w: The 1935 'hundred-step staircase' wing of the old Meguro Gajoen, seven lavishly painted banquet rooms open for seasonal exhibitions — often cited as a Spirited Away-like interior.

P.n: Ōmori Nori Museum (大森 海苔のふるさと館)
P.ad: Beside Ōmori Furusato-no-Hamabe Park, Ōta-ku, Tokyo
P.w: Free museum of Ōmori's centuries-old nori seaweed farming on Tokyo Bay, with a hands-on nori-making workshop and the old drying boats.

P.n: Kawasaki Daishi (川崎大師 平間寺)
P.w: Head temple of the Chizan school of Shingon (founded 1128), one of the Kantō's busiest at New Year, reached down a lane of candy-makers chopping sweets to a drumbeat.

P.n: Meguro Fudōson — Ryūsen-ji (目黒不動尊 瀧泉寺)
P.w: Temple founded in 808 by Jikaku Daishi — the oldest Fudō sanctuary in the Kantō, with a dragon-mouth waterfall for ascetic bathing and a hillside of halls.
Shrine and grave of Yoshida Shōin, the Bakumatsu teacher executed in 1859, with a replica of his Shōka Sonjuku school — at the head of the old-school Shōinjinja-dōri arcade on the Setagaya tram line.
Large 1678 Jōdo temple in Okusawa whose three halls hold nine seated Amida Buddhas — ginkgo and maple colour in autumn, a short walk from Jiyūgaoka.
Adachi's big park on the Nippori-Toneri liner — cherry groves, a lake and the spring nemophila fields lit up for the Flower and Light Movement.
Where Edward S. Morse spotted a Jōmon shell midden from the train in 1877 and began Japan's first modern archaeological dig — now a small riverside park with the original strata on view.

P.n: Tsukiji Outer Market (築地場外市場)
P.w: The 400-odd stalls and counters that stayed when the wholesale market moved to Toyosu — tamagoyaki on sticks, oysters, knives, kaisen-don and dried bonito, best before noon.
The vermilion lacquered bridge over the Daiya River at the gateway to Nikkō's shrines — part of Futarasan Shrine and the UNESCO Shrines and Temples of Nikkō.
The 700 m promenade above Edo Castle's moat under some 230 cherry trees — Tokyo's most beloved hanami walk, with rowboats on the water below and night illuminations in season.

P.ad: Takaomachi, by Takaosanguchi Station, Hachiōji, Tokyo 193-0844
P.w: Free nature museum at the foot of Mt Takao — a wall of mounted local wildlife and practical trail information before the climb.

Tokyo's city-history museum beside the Kokugikan, reopened 31 March 2026 after a four-year renovation — walk-through Nihonbashi bridge replica, Edo townscapes and a new full-scale Meiji Ginza Hattori clock shop.
Small museum on the shore of Shinobazu Pond recreating Taishō-era shitamachi life — a walk-in tenement row, merchant's shop and sweet stall; reopened March 2025 after a two-year renovation.

P.ad: Meiji Jingū Gaien, Kasumigaokamachi, Shinjuku-ku, Tokyo
P.w: The national stadium in the Meiji Jingū Gaien precinct, built for the Tokyo 2020 Olympics — see it from the Gaien ginkgo avenue side, or catch a match.

P.n: Haruki Murakami Library — Waseda International House of Literature
P.w: Waseda University's library and archive devoted to alumnus Haruki Murakami — opened 2021 on the Waseda campus; free to visit.
Waseda University's theatre museum, named for Shakespeare translator Tsubouchi Shōyō — Japanese and world theatre collections; free.
The national stage for noh and kyōgen in Sendagaya — check the programme for a performance.
Tokyo's metropolitan sports complex by Sendagaya Station — arena events plus a public pool and gym.
Big wooded park between Waseda and Shin-Ōkubo; its artificial hill Hakoneyama is the highest point in Tokyo's 23 wards — a short climb with a summit marker.
Edogawa green space with free-entry Japanese gardens and a small free zoo — an easy family stop in east Tokyo.
Old Kagurazaka shrine rebuilt in 2010 by Kengo Kuma — traditional form with glass doors that open a clear view into the main hall.
Wooden yose hall (1946) with tatami and chair seating — rakugo comic storytelling and iromono variety acts daily; a Shinjuku City cultural asset.

P.ad: Near Waseda Station (Tōzai Line), Shinjuku-ku, Tokyo
P.w: Museum on the site of Sōseki Sanbō, the house where the novelist of Kokoro and Botchan lived from 1907 until his death — his study, salon and veranda re-created.
Museum of the Mitsui family's collection of Japanese and East Asian art and tea utensils in Nihonbashi.

P.ad: Nihonbashi, Chūō-ku, Tokyo (by the Bank of Japan head office)
P.w: The Bank of Japan's free museum of Japanese money — from ancient coins and Edo gold koban to modern banknotes.
Old fishing-village island at the mouth of the Sumida, settled by Osaka fishermen in the early Edo period — it still keeps the canals and boat docks of the old fishing village.

P.ad: Uenokōen, Taitō-ku, Tokyo (south-west corner of Ueno Park)
P.w: Ueno Park's large pond at the park's south-west corner — a lakeside loop past the Shitamachi Museum.
Asakusa's tourist information centre facing Kaminarimon — free help desk for the Sensō-ji area.
Bunkyō shrine whose ~300 plum trees make the Feb 8 – Mar 8 ume festival one of Tokyo's favourite late-winter events.
Small shrine on Asakusa's northern edge said to be the birthplace of the maneki-neko beckoning cat; it enshrines the deity couple Izanagi and Izanami, so it's a magnet for love-luck prayers.

P.n: Super Potato Akihabara (スーパーポテト 秋葉原店)
P.ad: Kitabayashi Bldg 3F–5F, 1-11-2 Sotokanda, Chiyoda City, Tokyo 〒101-0021
P.w: Three floors of retro consoles, cartridges and memorabilia in a Mario-decorated building; Time Out calls the Akihabara flagship the chain's most famous location, 'almost like a museum'.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Retro video games — Akihabara's best-known shrine to Famicom/Super Famicom-era Nintendo, Sega and arcade culture · Retro-game shop

P.n: Mandarake Complex Akihabara (まんだらけコンプレックス)
P.w: Eight-storey flagship of the second-hand otaku chain, each floor sorted by product type — vintage 'Japanese Pop Antique' figures, magical-girl toys and cosplay, manga, dōjinshi and more (Time Out, Tokyo Cheapo).
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Anime & manga collectibles — the biggest single Mandarake, Akihabara's deep-cut used-figure and dōjinshi tower · Otaku megastore

P.n: The Gundam Base Tokyo (ガンダムベース東京)
P.ad: DiverCity Tokyo Plaza 7F, 1-1-10 Aomi, Kōtō City, Tokyo 〒135-0064
P.w: Bandai's official Gunpla (Gundam plastic-model) flagship: a shop zone with 2,000+ kits on sale, a replica of the Shizuoka factory line and a builders' zone (Time Out). Keeps operating after the Unicorn Gundam statue outside retired in Aug 2026.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Mobile Suit Gundam — Bandai's official Gunpla HQ shop, the pilgrimage stop for model builders · Gunpla flagship

P.n: Toshima City Tokiwasō Manga Museum (豊島区立トキワ荘マンガミュージアム)
P.w: A 2020 reconstruction of the Tokiwasō apartment where Tezuka Osamu, Fujiko Fujio and Ishinomori Shōtarō lived as young artists; the 2F recreates the 1950s–60s four-and-a-half-mat rooms and shared kitchen (GO TOKYO, japan-guide).
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Manga history — the 'sacred place' of postwar manga where Tezuka and the Doraemon/Cyborg 009 creators started out · Manga museum

P.n: Suginami Animation Museum (杉並アニメーションミュージアム)
P.ad: Suginami Kaikan 3F, 3-29-5 Kamiogi, Suginami City, Tokyo 〒167-0043
P.w: Free museum run by Tokyo Polytechnic University in the ward with Japan's densest cluster of anime studios; history-of-anime galleries, a dubbing booth, digital workshop, theatre and library (GO TOKYO, japan-guide).
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Anime industry — Japan's only museum devoted solely to animation, in the studio heartland of Suginami · Anime museum (free)

P.n: Suga Shrine stairs, Yotsuya (須賀神社 男坂)
P.ad: Suga Shrine (須賀神社), Sugachō, Yotsuya, Shinjuku City, Tokyo
P.w: The stone 'Otokozaka' staircase below Suga Shrine is where Taki and Mitsuha finally meet in the last scene of Shinkai Makoto's Your Name (2016) and on its poster; nippon.com calls it among the most famous seichi-junrei sites in Japan. Nearest station Yotsuya-sanchōme.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Your Name. (Kimi no Na wa) — the film's final-reunion staircase and poster image · Anime pilgrimage stairs

P.n: @home cafe Akihabara Main Branch (@ほぉ〜むカフェ 本店)
P.ad: Mitsuwa Building 4F/6F/7F, Sotokanda, Chiyoda City, Tokyo (Akihabara)
P.w: Japan's biggest and most popular maid-café chain (Time Out), with three floors of its main branch in Akihabara's Mitsuwa Building (Tokyo Cheapo); a newer flagship opened in Feb 2022 on 5F of Akiba Cultures Zone.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Akihabara otaku culture — the best-known maid café, the archetypal Akiba moe experience · Maid café

P.n: Pokémon Center Mega Tokyo, Ikebukuro (ポケモンセンターメガトウキョー)
P.ad: Sunshine City Alpa 2F, 3-1 Higashi-Ikebukuro, Toshima City, Tokyo
P.w: Pokémon's biggest Tokyo store (opened Dec 2014) on the 2nd floor of Sunshine City, with a store-exclusive Mega Charizard X statue; open 10:00–20:00, near Pikachu Sweets by Pokémon Café (GO TOKYO, Time Out).
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Pokémon — the 'Mega' flagship Pokémon Center with its exclusive Mega Charizard X statue · Pokémon flagship store

P.n: Sanrio Puroland (サンリオピューロランド)
P.ad: Tama Center (Tama New Town), Tama, Tokyo — by Tama-Center Station (Keiō / Odakyū / Tama Monorail)
P.w: Indoor theme park opened in 1990 in Tama New Town, half an hour from Shinjuku: a Hello Kitty musical, Kitty's house, live shows and meet-and-greets with My Melody, Cinnamoroll, Gudetama and Aggretsuko.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Hello Kitty & the Sanrio universe — the company's own indoor park ('Hello Kitty Land') · Character theme park

P.n: Kamakurakōkōmae Railway Crossing — Slam Dunk (鎌倉高校前 踏切)
P.ad: By Kamakurakōkōmae Station (Enoden line), Koshigoe, Kamakura, Kanagawa
P.w: The seaside Enoden level crossing just east of Kamakurakōkōmae Station, with the Pacific behind the passing tram — immortalised in the Slam Dunk opening and one of Japan's most-visited anime pilgrimage spots.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Slam Dunk — the railroad crossing from the anime's opening sequence · Anime pilgrimage spot

P.n: Animate Ikebukuro Flagship Store (アニメイト池袋本店)
P.w: Animate's flagship since 1983, expanded into ten floors of shops, event spaces, cafés and a theatre — recognised by Guinness World Records as the world's largest anime store, anchoring Ikebukuro's otaku quarter.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — All franchises — Guinness-certified largest anime store, the hub of Ikebukuro's Otome Road scene · Anime megastore

P.n: Ultraman Shopping Street, Soshigaya (ウルトラマン商店街)
P.ad: North of Soshigaya-Ōkura Station (Odakyū line), Soshigaya, Setagaya-ku, Tokyo
P.w: The everyday shopping street running north from Soshigaya-Ōkura Station is decked out with Ultraman statues and street lamps — Tsuburaya Productions, the studio behind Ultraman, was headquartered nearby.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Ultraman — tokusatsu hero honoured by the street beside Tsuburaya Productions' former home · Anime-themed shōtengai

P.n: Anime Tokyo Station, Ikebukuro (アニメ東京ステーション)
P.w: Opened October 2023 as Tokyo's official anime hub: a free basement archive of ~50,000 production items — layouts, storyboards, original drawings and cels rarely shown publicly — plus rotating exhibitions.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Cross-franchise — the Metropolitan Government-backed anime archive (current shows: Digimon Adventure 02 & Ojamajo Doremi 25th anniversary) · Free anime archive & gallery

P.n: Tokyo Anime Center, DNP Plaza Shibuya (東京アニメセンター)
P.ad: DNP Plaza Shibuya 2F, Jinnan, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo
P.w: Formerly in Akihabara and then Ichigaya, the Tokyo Anime Center now runs rotating anime, manga and game exhibitions with AR/VR on the second floor of DNP Plaza Shibuya; the shop is free to enter.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Rotating franchise exhibitions — the long-running official anime promotion centre · Anime exhibition space

P.n: Toei Animation Museum, Ōizumi (東映アニメーションミュージアム)
P.ad: Toei Animation Ōizumi Studio, Higashi-Ōizumi, Nerima-ku, Tokyo
P.w: Inside Toei Animation's Ōizumi studio in Nerima — the birthplace of Dragon Ball, Sailor Moon, One Piece and Pretty Cure — with exhibits on the studio's history and production.
P.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Toei Animation — Dragon Ball, Sailor Moon, One Piece, Precure; museum in the working studio · Studio museum

P.w: Tokyo's only natural ravine: a kilometre-long wooded path along the Yazawa River below street level, steps from Todoroki Station, ending at Todoroki Fudōson temple.
A riverside garden on the Edo River banks where some 50,000 irises of around 100 varieties bloom in June.

P.n: Nihombashi Mitsukoshi Main Store (日本橋三越本店)
P.w: Japan's first department store, descended from the 1673 Echigoya kimono shop; the 1935 building with its bronze lions and soaring atrium Tennyo (Goddess of Sincerity) statue is a nationally designated Important Cultural Property.

F.n: Chukasoba Ginza Hachigou (銀座 八五)
F.w: A tiny Ginza counter where a French-trained chef builds a clear, consommé-like shōyu chūka soba — Tokyo-style ramen at its most refined.
Roppongi branch of the Michelin-listed Iruca — a delicate shōyu ramen finished with a fragrant porcini oil.
Shinjuku-gyoemmae ramen counter (once Michelin-starred) famous for a hamaguri-clam and pork broth shio soba lifted with truffle and porcini.
Neighbourhood soba-ya in Shimo-Ochiai listed by Michelin for hand-made seiro soba.
Nishi-Azabu soba house in the Michelin selection — hand-made soba and seasonal sake-side dishes.

F.n: Sosakumenkobo Nakiryu (創作麺工房 鳴龍)
F.w: Ōtsuka counter that held a Michelin star for its Sichuan-inspired tantanmen; still Michelin-listed and still queued for.
The cult tonkatsu that made pale, rosy low-temperature frying famous — Michelin-listed, long queues.
Yotsuya-area tonkatsu counter, a Michelin Bib Gourmand for its carefully fried branded-pork rosu and hire.
Takadanobaba tonkatsu shop on the Michelin Bib Gourmand list — juicy, lightly-crumbed hire and rosu.
Ikegami neighbourhood tonkatsu near Honmon-ji, a Michelin Bib Gourmand.
Musashi-Koyama tonkatsu built on 'mochibuta' pork, a Michelin Bib Gourmand.
Ueno tonkatsu house in the Michelin Bib Gourmand selection.
Ikejiri-Ōhashi ramen shop whose silky shrimp-and-pork wonton-men in a white or black shōyu broth draws daily queues; Michelin Bib Gourmand.
Mikawashima/Nippori ramen-ya on the Michelin Bib Gourmand list for its clean chicken-based shio and shōyu bowls.

F.n: Homemade Ramen Muginae (自家製麺 麦苗)
F.w: Ōmori ramen shop making its own noodles daily — a Michelin Bib Gourmand and a ramen-otaku pilgrimage.
Back-street Ginza ramen counter whose shio ramen won a Michelin Bib Gourmand in the 2026 guide — an affordable bowl a block from the luxury flagships.
Takaido shop devoted to shio (salt) soba, a Michelin Bib Gourmand.
Yotsuya-sanchōme ramen shop with a Michelin Bib Gourmand in the 2026 guide.
Zaiyu Hasegawa's playful modern kaiseki — the famous 'Dentucky' chicken wing and a warmth that made it one of Tokyo's best-loved tables.
Yoshihiro Narisawa's 'innovative satoyama' cuisine — forest, sea and soil of Japan on the plate, opening with bread that rises and bakes at the table.

F.ad: 2F Azabudai Hills Garden Plaza D, 5-10-7 Toranomon, Minato-ku, Tokyo 105-0001
F.w: Hiroyasu Kawate's counter-theatre French tasting menu, relocated to Azabudai Hills.
Fumio Kondo's Ginza counter, the master of vegetable tempura — the slow-fried sweet potato is the signature.
Masahiro Yoshitake's top-tier Ginza Edomae sushi counter.

F.n: Kagurazaka Ishikawa (神楽坂 石かわ)
F.w: Hideki Ishikawa's kaiseki house tucked in a Kagurazaka back alley — the benchmark of Tokyo seasonal cooking.

F.n: Nodaiwa Azabu Iikura Honten (野田岩 麻布飯倉本店)
F.w: Fifth-generation unagi house in an old kura-style building near Tokyo Tower — wild-eel kabayaki in the Edo manner.

F.n: Onigiri Asakusa Yadoroku (おにぎり浅草宿六)
F.w: Tokyo's oldest onigiri shop (1954) — rice balls pressed to order at a tiny counter behind Sensō-ji; a Michelin Bib Gourmand and a dawn-queue favourite.
Yoshinori Watanabe's riverside French dining room in Komagata, Asakusa — Michelin one-star cooking looking across the Sumida to Skytree.
Noboru Arai's French restaurant in the back streets of Kannon-ura, Asakusa — two Michelin stars in the 2026 guide.
Small soba-ya near Kappabashi, a Michelin Bib Gourmand in the 2026 guide.
Michelin-listed Japanese counter in Kannon-ura, north of Sensō-ji.
Michelin-listed neighbourhood shokudō in Asakusa serving Japanese home-style set meals.
Soba-ya just below Kanda Myōjin, in the 2026 Michelin selection — Kanda's soba tradition in a new generation.
Okachimachi yōshoku house (1905) credited with Tokyo's tonkatsu lineage — lard-fried katsuretsu; a Michelin Bib Gourmand.
Unagi specialist by Tokyo Station's Yaesu side, a Michelin Bib Gourmand.

F.n: Japanese Ramen Gokan (Japanese Ramen 五感)
F.w: Ikebukuro ramen shop with a Michelin Bib Gourmand in the 2026 guide.

F.ad: 1F Toranomon Hills Residential Tower, 1-1-1 Atago, Minato-ku, Tokyo 105-0002
F.w: Hiroyuki Kanda's eight-seat counter — three Michelin stars every year since the first Tokyo guide, now in Toranomon Hills.
Minami-Aoyama contemporary French in the Michelin selection — a relaxed, good-value tasting menu.
Asakusa Edomae sushi counter in the Michelin selection.
Shibuya basement shokudō built around bonito flakes shaved to order over rice and miso soup; Michelin Bib Gourmand 2026.
Ginza tonkatsu counter serving a prix-fixe of rare cuts — new Michelin Bib Gourmand 2026.
Yakitori bar run by two brothers in Higashi-Mukōjima, skewers mostly served salted — new Michelin Bib Gourmand 2026.
Shirokane yōshoku house with nostalgic hamburg steak in demi-glace — new Michelin Bib Gourmand 2026.

F.ad: 7F Four Seasons Hotel Tokyo at Marunouchi, 1-11-1 Marunouchi, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo 100-6277
F.w: Daniel Calvert's dining room above Tokyo Station — awarded three Michelin stars in the 18th Tokyo guide, French technique with Japanese ingredients.
Meguro-station yakitori counter on the Michelin Bib Gourmand list.

F.n: Jimbocho Gokita (神保町 五木田)
F.w: Jimbōchō 'neo-yakitori' — skewers paired with French sauces; Michelin-listed 2026.

F.n: Bird Land Ginza (バードランド 銀座)
F.w: Toshihiro Wada's basement yakitori under Ginza 4-chōme — the restaurant that took yakitori into the Michelin guide.
Oshiage yakitori counter in the shadow of Skytree, listed in the Michelin guide.
Kagurazaka-side yakitori bar, Michelin Bib Gourmand 2026.

F.n: Asagaya Bird Land (阿佐ヶ谷 バードランド)
F.w: The Asagaya original of the Bird Land yakitori family, in the Michelin selection.
Ginza Japanese restaurant newly awarded one Michelin star.
Shirokanedai basement tempura counter, one Michelin star in the 2026 guide.
Kagurazaka tempura counter in the Michelin selection.
Toru Okuda's Ginza kaiseki house — two Michelin stars in the 2026 guide.
Azabu-Jūban unagi specialist in the Michelin selection.

F.n: Sobakappo Nagano (蕎麦割烹 長野)
F.w: Higashi-Mukōjima soba-kappō — soba plus platters of small dishes made for sake; new Michelin Bib Gourmand 2026.
Ginza tempura shop in the Michelin selection with affordable lunch tempura (¥1,500–9,000).
Yoshinaga Jinbo's modern Italian that 'paints scenes of the fields on the plate' — Michelin-listed.
Gaienmae basement Japanese where char-grilled fish and rice cooked in an iron pot are the mainstays — Michelin-listed.

F.n: Nihombashi Kakigaracho Sugita (日本橋蛎殻町 すぎた)
F.w: Takaaki Sugita's basement Edomae counter, among Tokyo's hardest reservations — two Michelin stars.
Edogawabashi unagi house in an old wooden building, Michelin-listed.
Unagi house founded in 1835 and run by the sixth generation — continuous since the shogunate; Michelin-listed.
Shintomi Edomae sushi counter near Tsukiji — one Michelin star in the 2026 guide.
Nishi-Ogikubo ramen shop milling its own noodles — Michelin Bib Gourmand 2026.
Shintomi sushi counter in the Michelin selection, a short walk from the Tsukiji outer market.

F.n: Sukiyabashi Jiro Honten (すきやばし次郎 本店)
F.ad: B1F Tsukamoto Sogyo Bldg, 4-2-15 Ginza, Chūō-ku, Tokyo 104-0061
F.w: Jiro Ono's ten-seat counter in a Ginza subway-side basement, made world-famous by 'Jiro Dreams of Sushi' — dropped from Michelin only because it stopped taking public bookings.

F.n: Kanda Yabu Soba (かんだやぶそば)
F.w: The patriarch of Tokyo's Yabu soba lineage (1880) — rebuilt as a one-storey house after the 2013 fire; staff still sing orders to the kitchen.
Soba house since 1884 in a Taishō-era wooden building a minute from Awajichō Station — more down-to-earth and cheaper than Yabu, just as beloved.
Tokyo's only anko-nabe specialist, cooking monkfish hotpot since 1830 in a 1930 wooden house — no reservations, no cards, open in the cold season.
Serving loach simmered in a shallow iron pan since 1801 — the Edo working-man's unagi — at low tables on a tatami floor by the Sumida.
Ginza yōshoku house since 1895 — credited with the first omelette rice (1900) and the menchi-katsu minced-meat cutlet; still serving both.
Nihonbashi yōshoku pioneer (1931) whose soft-centred omurice was created for Juzo Itami's film 'Tampopo' and named after it.
One of Japan's oldest bars (1880), founded by wine pioneer Kamiya Denbei, inventor of the sweet Denki Bran still poured by the glass to a crowd of regulars.
Tokyo's most famous tofu restaurant, founded in the Edo period by a tofu-maker brought from Kyoto by Kan'ei-ji's imperial abbot — silken tofu in sweet ankake sauce, by Uguisudani Station.

F.n: Shin-Yokohama Rāmen Museum (新横浜ラーメン博物館)
F.w: The world's first food theme park (1994) — a 1958 Shōwa street set underground with nine branches of famous regional ramen shops serving mini bowls.
Kawagoe's 'Penny Candy Lane' — a Shōwa-era alley of a dozen old sweet shops selling dagashi, sweet-potato treats and metre-long fu-gashi.
A century-old tea house on the Taishakuten approach — the 'Tora-san' films' dango shop — serving fresh mugwort kusa-dango with red-bean paste.
Hiroo tempura counter led by Shigeyoshi Uchitsu — one Michelin star in the 2025 guide, light batter that lets each vegetable speak.
Ebisu French restaurant devoted to the sea — one Michelin star in the 2026 guide.
Iriya tempura counter in the Michelin selection, a quiet stop between Ueno and Minowa.
Ebisu-side neighbourhood bistro in the Michelin selection.

F.n: Tempura Motoyoshi (てんぷら 元吉)
F.w: Ebisu tempura counter — two Michelin stars in the 2026 guide.
Moto-Azabu tempura counter — one Michelin star in the 2026 guide.
Ebisu Italian with a Michelin Bib Gourmand in the 2026 guide.

F.n: Tsukishima Monja Street (月島もんじゃストリート)
F.w: Tokyo's own griddle dish on its home street — some 75 monjayaki shops line Nishinaka-dōri, where you scrape the crisping batter off the teppan with tiny spatulas.
Kagurazaka soba-ya with a Michelin Bib Gourmand in the 2026 guide.
Quiet back-street soba-ya behind Omotesandō, in the 2026 Michelin selection.

F.n: Ginza Yondaime Takahashiya (銀座 四代目 高橋屋)
F.w: Ginza outpost of an unagi house founded in Sugito, Saitama, in 1873 — Michelin-listed.
Ginza counter cooking everything over firewood (makiyaki) — Michelin-listed.

F.n: Ginza Shinohara (銀座 しのはら)
F.w: Takemasa Shinohara's Ginza kaiseki counter — two Michelin stars in the 2026 guide.
Nishi-Azabu soba-ya, a Michelin Bib Gourmand in the 2026 guide.
Nakameguro ramen shop known for broad, springy hand-made noodles — new Michelin Bib Gourmand 2026.
Single-item shop founded in 1717 beside Chōmei-ji — credited as the birthplace of sakura-mochi, the pink mochi of red-bean paste wrapped in pickled cherry leaves.

F.ad: By Kototoi Bridge, Mukōjima 5-chōme, Sumida-ku, Tokyo 131-0033
F.w: Late-Edo dango shop by the Kototoi Bridge, founded to feed cherry-blossom and fireworks crowds on the Sumida — three-colour bean-paste dumplings.

F.ad: Ebisu 1-chōme (beside the Shibuya River), Shibuya-ku, Tokyo 150-0013
F.w: The original Afuri by the Shibuya River — the light, citrusy yuzu shio ramen that became a Tokyo signature, ordered from a ticket machine.
Lunch-only soba shop in a quiet Nerima residential street serving a sobazen set of fine soba, appetisers and soba-gaki — new Michelin Bib Gourmand 2026.
Nakano soba-ya serving delicately thin 100% buckwheat seiro soba and stone-ground inaka soba with appetisers — new Michelin Bib Gourmand 2026.
Kanda basement that serves only biryani — mutton or chicken, cooked dum-style — and won a Michelin Bib Gourmand in the 2026 guide.
Yotsuya-area Chinese kitchen known for Cantonese flame-broiled dishes — new Michelin Bib Gourmand 2026.
Setagaya trattoria cooking Italy's regional dishes — pici with tomato ragù is the signature; new Michelin Bib Gourmand 2026.
Ogikubo-area shop devoted to Hakodate's clear salt ramen — a Michelin Bib Gourmand in the 2026 guide.
Soshigaya osteria of simple handmade pasta and chargrilled fish and meat — new Michelin Bib Gourmand 2026.
Ōta ramen shop building its bowl on shijimi clams from Shimane's Lake Shinji — a Michelin Bib Gourmand in the 2026 guide.
Ningyōchō chicken house (1760) credited in one account with inventing oyakodon in the 1880s — lunch queues for the bowl, chicken sukiyaki at night.
Yotsuya-area neighbourhood sushi counter with a Michelin Bib Gourmand in the 2026 guide — rare good-value Edomae nigiri.

F.ad: Kichijōji-Minamichō, at the entrance to Inokashira Park, Musashino, Tokyo
F.w: Smoky yakitori institution on this spot since 1928 — the last stop before Inokashira Park, with cheap skewers and beer for walkers and families.

F.ad: Old Tōkaidō road near Hatajuku, Hakone, Kanagawa
F.w: Thatched teahouse on the Old Tōkaidō stone road, run by the same family for some 400 years — warm amazake and mochi for hikers between Hatajuku and Lake Ashi.
Basement sushi counter in Kamiyamachō (Oku-Shibuya) where you order single pieces off the blackboard — a Michelin Bib Gourmand, so a counter-sushi meal without the omakase bill.
Ex-DJ chef Takuro Yanase's Meguro counter — a pure, clear chicken shōyu ramen loaded with two kinds of pork, wontons and fried onion. Michelin Bib Gourmand 2026.
Koishikawa unagi house near Kōrakuen — one of the Michelin Guide's picks for Tokyo's Edo-style freshwater eel, and a Bib Gourmand.
Small, old-school Asakusa eel shop a few steps from Kaminarimon — a Michelin Bib Gourmand and one of the guide's Tokyo unagi picks.
Basement eel restaurant just outside Mejiro Station — a Michelin Bib Gourmand and one of the guide's Tokyo unagi picks.
Graceful old-school Ryōgoku soba house near the Edo-Tokyo Museum; the chef scours Japan for buckwheat, and the big anago tempura is a Michelin inspectors' favourite dish. Bib Gourmand 2026.
Shimbashi tempura counter for rice bowls and set meals — the signature kakiage-don of crisp shrimp fritters is a Michelin inspectors' iconic-Tokyo-dish pick. Bib Gourmand 2026.
Ningyōchō tonkatsu in a refurbished old house fitted out with recycled wood — loin and fillet set meals, à la carte or courses. Bib Gourmand 2026 and a Michelin inspectors' iconic-dish pick.
Drop-in, affordable sushi next to the National Art Center, named for and best at the shimmering blue-skinned fish — kohada and saba. A Michelin inspectors' iconic-Tokyo-dish pick.

Kappo-style Toranomon counter where the server cooks alternating slices of beef and vegetables in front of you; the meringue-whipped egg dip is the twist. A Michelin inspectors' iconic-Tokyo-dish pick.
Chef Hidetoshi Nakamura's Nishi-Azabu kaiseki — Tokyo's newest three-star (MICHELIN Guide Tokyo 2026); the clam-and-gomadōfu clear soup was an inspectors' dish of the year.
Akasaka sushi counter whose whole salt-grilled sweetfish nigiri was one of the Michelin inspectors' 2026 dishes of the year.
Shiba sushi-ya whose thick, soft harakami tuna nigiri — the star topping of Edo sushi — was a Michelin inspectors' favourite dish of 2025.
Sasazuka stand-up sushi bar serving nigiri only — the Edo-era tachigui format, and a Michelin Bib Gourmand since the 2025 Tokyo guide.
Takadanobaba basement fry shop — tonkatsu and yōshoku cutlets; new Michelin Bib Gourmand in the 2025 Tokyo guide.
Mita neighbourhood sushi counter that made the Michelin Bib Gourmand list in 2025 and kept it in 2026 — counter sushi at Bib prices.
Second-floor Japanese-cuisine counter in Yotsuya's Arakichō backstreets, added to the Michelin Guide in 2024.
Yoyogi grill house focused on yakiton — grilled pork skewers — with the meat-stuffed green peppers kept on since the first generation. Michelin Bib Gourmand 2026.
Small-plates (koryōri) restaurant in Shibuya's Higashi whose signature is duck: salt-grilled, as a chilled breast stew in summer and as hot jibuni in winter. Michelin Bib Gourmand 2026.
Asakusa yōshoku grill — Japanese-Western comfort food; the beef stew is the best-seller and the omurice comes with demi-glace or ketchup. Michelin Bib Gourmand 2026.
Ningyōchō tempura counter holding one Michelin star in the 2026 Tokyo guide.
Kōenji tempura counter famous for its tempura soft-boiled egg on rice — and for the chef tossing eggshells with kabuki flourish. Michelin Bib Gourmand 2026; Time Out-listed.
Nakano sushi counter of zelkova wood; the founder trained in Kyōbashi and inherited the name — old-school toppings on red-vinegar rice. Michelin Bib Gourmand 2026.
Nishi-Azabu sushi counter promoted from one to two Michelin stars in the 2026 Tokyo guide.
Akasaka Japanese-cuisine counter — clear-broth wanmono to house-made soba; new one Michelin star in the 2026 Tokyo guide.
Hiroo Japanese restaurant awarded a first Michelin star in the 2026 Tokyo guide.
Kagurazaka-side sushi counter (Fukuromachi) awarded a first Michelin star in the 2026 Tokyo guide.
Minami-Azabu sushi counter awarded a first Michelin star in the 2026 Tokyo guide.
Minami-Aoyama Japanese restaurant promoted to two Michelin stars in 2026; its spring sea-bream sashimi on cherry-blossom-cut Edo kiriko glass was an inspectors' dish of the year.
Hiroo sushi counter holding one Michelin star in the 2026 Tokyo guide.
Nihombashi yakitori counter promoted to one Michelin star in the 2025 Tokyo guide for precisely grilled chicken.
Meguro (Higashiyama) Japanese restaurant awarded one Michelin star in the 2025 Tokyo guide.
Atago shōjin-ryōri restaurant — the vegetarian cuisine of Buddhist monks — holding one Michelin star in the 2025 Tokyo guide.
Hiroo sushi counter first starred in the 2024 Michelin Tokyo guide.
Arakichō (Yotsuya) crab specialist first starred in the 2024 Michelin Tokyo guide.
Minami-Aoyama Japanese restaurant first starred in the 2024 Michelin Tokyo guide.
Kagurazaka-side (Fukuromachi) Japanese restaurant with one Michelin star.
Ginza Japanese restaurant holding one Michelin star in the 2026 guide.
Nishi-Azabu Japanese restaurant first starred in the 2024 Michelin Tokyo guide.

Soba house a short walk from Suitengū with a wide soba-mae spread — sake snacks and hot tempura from the counter before the noodles. Michelin Bib Gourmand 2026 and one of Michelin's six Tokyo soba-mae picks.

F.ad: Yamatoya Bldg 9F, 1-13-7 Nishishinjuku, Shinjuku City, Tokyo
F.w: Hiroyasu Kayama's apothecary-style bar with no printed menu — cocktails built from herbs and botanicals, many grown on his family farm in Saitama. World's 50 Best Bars 2025 No 18 and Asia's 50 Best No 9.

F.n: Virtù, Four Seasons Hotel Tokyo at Otemachi
F.ad: Four Seasons Hotel Tokyo at Otemachi, 1-2-1 Otemachi, Chiyoda City, Tokyo 100-0004 (hotel address per Google Hotels; bar floor not confirmed)
F.w: Art-deco cocktail bar at the Four Seasons Otemachi; the Virtù Martini uses Japanese gin and vodka with hinoki bitters. Asia's 50 Best Bars 2026 No 26 and World's 50 Best Bars 2025.

F.ad: The Tokyo EDITION, Ginza, 2-8-13 Ginza, Chuo City, Tokyo 104-0061 (mezzanine lobby) — address from Google search summary
F.w: Punch bar inside The Tokyo EDITION, Ginza, serving shared punch bowls reworked with Japanese spirits (Big Red Dot: Akadama, Nikka Coffey Malt, awamori). Asia's 50 Best Bars 2026 No 23.

F.ad: Basement, Nishi-Ikebukuro, Toshima City, Tokyo (exact street number not found in results)
F.w: Unsigned basement bar in Nishi-Ikebukuro, a fixture for 14+ years, with inventive cocktails built on Japanese ingredients such as a soba-tea Screwdriver. Asia's 50 Best Bars 2026 No 39.
Shibuya cocktail bar whose Yakiniku Bloody (smoked vodka, wagyu fat, yellow tomato, black garlic) shows its Japanese-food-inspired drinks; first entry on World's 50 Best Bars in 2025 at No 48.

F.ad: Ginza, Chuo City, Tokyo (basement; exact address not in results)
F.w: Hidetsugu Ueno's Ginza basement institution with 'no menu' bespoke cocktails and hand-carved ice; regulars come for the White Lady. Long-time World's 50 Best Bars entry.

F.ad: Dis Ebisu Bldg 102, 1-5-8 Ebisunishi, Shibuya City, Tokyo 150-0021
F.w: Small Ebisu bar devoted to absinthe and herbal liqueurs, open since 2010; try the Sazerac Highball. Asia's 50 Best Bars 2026 extended list (No 53).
'Coffee only' Ginza kissaten opened in 1948 by Ichiro Sekiguchi, famous for aged coffee beans — old-crop beans kept for a decade or more in date-marked jars.

F.ad: Shibuya, Shibuya City, Tokyo (3-min walk from Shibuya Stn; exact address not in results)
F.w: Hushed, antique-filled Shibuya kissaten revered for hand-drip coffee and its tall chiffon cake; it inspired Blue Bottle's founder. Cash only.

F.ad: Kiyosumi-Shirakawa, Koto City, Tokyo (renovated warehouse; exact address not in results)
F.w: Eiichi Kunitomo's coffee 'omakase' in a converted Kiyosumi-Shirakawa warehouse — tasting courses of pour-over, cold brew and coffee cocktails served at a counter.

F.ad: Kayamura Bldg 1F (香村ビル１階), 3-16 Kanda Nishikicho, Chiyoda City, Tokyo 101-0054
F.w: Light-roast specialty roaster in Kanda-Nishikichō pouring about 15 single origins by hand drip; owner Kiyokazu Suzuki is a former Japan AeroPress champion.
Oslo café-bar's first overseas branch (2012) in Tomigaya: light-roast Nordic coffee by day, cocktails by night, in a vintage Scandinavian interior.

F.ad: 2-14-1 Kamimeguro, Meguro City, Tokyo (per Time Out; postcode not in result)
F.w: Neighbourhood roastery in a small two-storey house beside the Tokyu tracks in Nakameguro — espresso and hand drip from house-roasted beans.

F.ad: 1-2-6 Nishi-Shinjuku, Shinjuku City, Tokyo (Omoide Yokocho; per Time Out; postcode not in result)
F.w: Kissaten in Shinjuku's Omoide Yokochō since 1964: cloth-filter hand-drip coffee from hand-sorted house-roasted beans, plus coffee jelly with cream.

F.n: Nonbei Yokochō, Shibuya (渋谷のんべい横丁)
F.w: 'Drunkard's Alley' beside the Shibuya tracks: a 1950s-era yokochō of around 39 tiny bars and eateries, some seating only four or five, dominated by yakitori shops.

F.n: Harmonica Yokochō, Kichijōji (ハモニカ横丁)
F.ad: Kichijōji Honchō 1-chōme (north exit of Kichijōji Station), Musashino, Tokyo
F.w: Postwar black-market warren of covered lanes north of Kichijōji Station, named for its harmonica-reed rows of tiny shops; by night some 56 hole-in-the-wall bars and yakitori counters under red lanterns.

F.n: Hoppy Street, Asakusa (ホッピー通り)
F.w: An ~80 m strip of old-school open-air izakaya west of Sensō-ji, nicknamed 'Stew Street' for its bowls of beef nikomi, many still pouring Hoppy, the postwar beer-substitute mixed with shochu.

F.n: Beer Club Popeye, Ryōgoku (麦酒倶楽部ポパイ)
F.w: Tatsuo Aoki's pioneering Ryōgoku beer bar, long regarded as Tokyo's essential craft-beer pilgrimage: 70+ taps kept in impeccable condition, mostly from Japanese breweries, plus real ales on hand pump and its own small brewery.

F.n: Beer Bar Ushitora, Shimokitazawa (うしとら)
F.ad: 6-3-27 Daita, Setagaya-ku, Tokyo (Tokyo Cheapo; Time Out lists 2F, 2-9-3 Kitazawa — confirm)
F.w: Shimokitazawa's 'high temple of craft beer' and Tokyo taproom of Tochigi's Ushitora Brewery: 35 taps, at least seven of them house brews, with izakaya-style snacks.

F.n: Gem by Moto, Ebisu (ジェムバイモト)
F.w: Marie Chiba's counter-only Ebisu sake specialist pouring boutique sake from across Japan with seasonal small plates designed to match; reservations recommended.

Classic izakaya in business since 1925, with a long cedar counter, a master in happi coat and headband, and serious sake from a family in the sake trade for generations; house speciality kitsune raclette. Selected for Tabelog's Izakaya Hyakumeiten (EAST) 2024 and 2025.
Long-running Yoyogi-Uehara izakaya overseen by an English-speaking sake sommelier, with a well-chosen nihonshu list kept in glass fridges behind the counter and English drink menus.

F.n: Yūrakuchō Gādo-shita, under the tracks (有楽町ガード下)
F.ad: Brick arches under the JR Yamanote Line either side of Yūrakuchō Station, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo
F.w: Salaryman drinking strip built into the brick arches beneath the Yamanote Line ('gādo-shita', below the girder), running nearly 700 m either side of Yūrakuchō Station: yakitori joints and izakaya with trains rumbling overhead.

F.n: Harukiya Ogikubo Honten (春木屋 荻窪本店)
F.ad: Kamiogi, Suginami-ku, Tokyo (Ōme-kaidō, north side of Ogikubo Station) — street number not confirmed
F.w: Opened 1949 and the standard-bearer of Ogikubo/Tokyo-style ramen: chūka soba blending chicken and fish stock with soy sauce, plus wantanmen and tsukemen, noodles made fresh each morning (Time Out). Ramen Adventures praises the wantanmen's broth.

F.n: Fuunji Shinjuku Honten (風雲児 新宿本店)
F.ad: Hokuto Dai-ichi Bldg. 1F, 2-14-3 Yoyogi, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo
F.w: Time Out calls it the place to go for tsukemen near Shinjuku: a thick, creamy chicken-and-fish double soup with straight noodles and queues day and night. Listed in Tabelog's Ramen Hyakumeiten TOKYO 2025.

F.ad: Koenjiminami, Suginami-ku, Tokyo — street number not confirmed
F.w: Michelin Bib Gourmand udon house in Kōenji: freshly kneaded, freshly boiled udon from domestic wheat in a kombu-and-dried-sardine sauce, with à la carte dishes in the evening.

Shin-Koiwa shop that Time Out and The Infatuation name among Tokyo's best tsukemen: a rich dried-fish, pork-bone and chicken soup with chāshū and tsukune toppings. A Tabelog Ramen Hyakumeiten TOKYO 2025 selection.

Hailed as the ancestor of abura soba and serving the same menu since 1965 near Musashi-Sakai Station: medium-thick noodles over a meaty sauce, topped with menma, chāshū and naruto, dressed with house chili oil and vinegar (Time Out).

F.ad: Kameari, Katsushika-ku, Tokyo — street number not confirmed
F.w: Kameari tsukemen specialist with its own Ramen Adventures listing and a place in Tokyo Cheapo's top-10 Tokyo tsukemen restaurants.

Century-old Ueno wagashi shop widely cited as one of Tokyo's three great dorayaki makers; the Japan Times profiled it as one of the two shops claiming to have created the dorayaki. Its dorayaki uses aged azuki paste in a honey-infused batter.
Opened in Azabu-Jūban in 1909 and, per the Japan Times, the shop popularly credited with originating taiyaki; also on Time Out's best-taiyaki list.

F.n: Toraya Akasaka flagship (とらや 赤坂店)
F.w: Flagship of Toraya, the 500-year-old former Imperial Court confectioner, rebuilt in 2018 by architect Hiroshi Naito with a shop, factory, Toraya café and gallery; the signature is yōkan.
Monaka maker founded in 1884 in Ueno Ikenohata and in Ginza since the war; its monaka appears in Natsume Sōseki's 'I Am a Cat' and must usually be reserved in advance.
Japan's oldest bakery, which created the anpan in 1874 using sake yeast; its sakura anpan was presented to Emperor Meiji.
Yanaka kakigōri specialist shaving natural Nikkō ice on a hand-cranked machine, with natural syrups and fresh fruit; unusually it serves kakigōri year-round.

F.ad: Asakusa, Taitō-ku, Tokyo (main shop near Sensō-ji; Kaminarimon branch also)
F.w: Asakusa fixture since 1945 that sells essentially one thing — a crisp-topped jumbo melonpan best eaten warm, often sold out by 4pm.

F.n: Bricolage Bread & Co. (ブリコラージュ ブレッド アンド カンパニー)
F.w: Roppongi bakery-café from L'Effervescence chef Shinobu Namae, baker Ayumu Iwanaga and Fuglen's Kenji Kojima; signature deep-crusted Bricolage loaf from ancient grains. Selected for Tabelog Bread TOKYO Hyakumeiten 2026.

F.n: Pokémon Café Tokyo, Nihonbashi (ポケモンカフェ 日本橋)
F.ad: Nihonbashi Takashimaya S.C. East Building 5F, Nihonbashi, Chūō City, Tokyo (with Pokémon Center Tokyo DX)
F.w: The world's first Pokémon Café (2018), beside Pokémon Center Tokyo DX; reopened 17 June 2026 after renovation with Pikachu curry, Eevee pancakes, the new Pika Pika Parfait and a live Chef Pikachu show — the Gengar smoothie stays.
F.k: ★ Anime & pop culture — Pokémon — the franchise's original themed café, reservation-only, with a live Pikachu show

F.n: Rokurinsha, Tokyo Ramen Street (六厘舎 東京ラーメンストリート)
F.ad: Tokyo Ramen Street, Tokyo Station First Avenue B1 (Yaesu side), Marunouchi, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo
F.w: The star of Tokyo Station's eight-shop Tokyo Ramen Street and by far its longest queue — thick tsukemen noodles dipped into a dense pork-and-seafood broth simmered for 13 hours.

F.n: Chūkamen-ten Kiraku, Dōgenzaka (中華麺店 喜楽)
F.w: A Dōgenzaka relic serving Tokyo-style noodles since 1952 — shōyu ramen with chewy noodles and crisp fried onions, regulars coming back for decades.

F.n: Tsukemen Gonokami Seisakusho (つけ麺 五ノ神製作所)
F.ad: Sendagaya, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo (by Shinjuku Station south side)
F.w: Queues form an hour before opening for this shrimp-obsessed tsukemen counter, whose creamy shrimp-miso and shrimp-tomato dips are built from hundreds of kilos of otherwise-wasted shrimp shells.
Founded in 1946 as the first Hakata-style ramen shop in the Kantō region; a late-night Nishi-Azabu institution for milky tonkotsu and ultra-thin flat noodles.

F.n: Shibire Noodles Rousokuya, Ginza (SHIBIRE NOODLE 蝋燭屋)
F.w: A chic Ginza noodle bar run by a former Chinese-restaurant chef, specialising in ma-la heat: mabo ramen crowned with numbing mapo tofu.

F.n: Ramenya Shima, Nishi-Shinjuku (らぁ麺や 嶋)
F.w: Ranked No 1 on Ramen Adventures' best-100 for 2025 and a fixture of Tabelog's Tokyo top three — queues once began at 7am; the rustic shōyu ramen is the bowl to get.

F.n: Chūka Soba Shibata, Komae (中華そば しば田)
F.w: A celebrated chūka-soba champion that relocated to Komae; its duck-and-seafood double soup and punchy soy tare put it at No 4 on Ramen Adventures' 2025 Tokyo best-100.

F.n: Chūka Soba Kamofuku, Hachiōji (中華そば 鴨福)
F.ad: Hachiōji, Tokyo (15 min walk from Hachiōji Station)
F.w: Western Tokyo's most raved-about ramen of 2024 per Time Out and No 5 on Ramen Adventures' 2025 best-100 — worth the trek from Hachiōji Station for its duck-and-Shamo chūka soba.

F.n: Kirby Café Tokyo, Tokyo Solamachi (カービィカフェ)
F.ad: Tokyo Solamachi 4F, Tokyo Skytree Town, Oshiage, Sumida-ku, Tokyo
F.w: Nintendo's pink hero gets his own café on Solamachi's fourth floor under Skytree — Kirby-shaped burgers and pizza, most dishes and drinks served with a collectible, plus an exclusive-goods shop.
